content: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a condition characterized by a three-dimensional deformity of the spine. While AIS often progresses during periods of growth and can result in visible surface deformities, it is typically not associated with symptoms. However, when the spinal curvature exceeds a critical threshold, there is an increased risk of health complications and further progression of the curve. To prevent the progression of AIS, various interventions are employed, including scoliosis-specific exercises, bracing, and surgical procedures. The primary goals of these interventions are to correct the spinal deformity, prevent further worsening of the curvature, restore trunk symmetry and balance, and minimize associated morbidity and pain. These measures aim to allow individuals to return to full functional capacity. Surgery is generally recommended for individuals with spinal curvatures exceeding 40 to 50 degrees. The objective of surgical intervention is to halt the progression of the curvature while improving trunk balance and cosmetic appearance. Short-term outcomes of surgical treatment for AIS have demonstrated improvements in several clinical measures. However, there is a significant lack of data regarding the long-term outcomes of surgical treatment in individuals with AIS. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of surgical versus non-surgical interventions in individuals with AIS who have severe spinal curves exceeding 45 degrees. The focus was on outcomes such as trunk balance, scoliosis progression, cosmetic concerns, quality of life, disability, psychological well-being, back pain, and adverse effects, both in the short term (a few months) and the long term (over 20 years). To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Back Review Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and four additional databases, as well as three trial registries. The search was conducted up to August 2014 without language restrictions. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed, and an extensive hand search of grey literature was undertaken. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective controlled trials that compared spinal fusion surgery with non-surgical interventions in individuals with AIS and a Cobb angle greater than 45 degrees. The review focused on all types of instrumented surgical interventions involving spinal fusion that aimed to correct the curvature and stabilize the spine. Despite the extensive search, no RCTs or prospective controlled trials meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. Consequently, no evidence was found comparing surgical and non-surgical interventions for AIS in individuals with severe curves exceeding 45 degrees. In conclusion, due to the absence of relevant studies, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the comparative effectiveness of surgical versus non-surgical interventions for AIS in individuals with severe spinal curvatures.
